=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer position

**Do not accept this as a balanced package.** The Seller is combining broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with limits applying to virtually every claim. The result could be that Wattlebridge acquires known problems but has neither a completion protection nor an effective post-completion remedy.

The priorities are to protect the AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free economics, secure key consents and releases before Completion, and preserve meaningful recourse.

This review is based on the Seller’s summaries and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying DD documents or full SPA. The drafting and source documents need to be checked before agreeing final positions.

## 1. Liability limitations: reject a single regime for all claims

### General warranty cap and thresholds
The proposed AUD 4.8 million cap is 20% of price. That is a commercial negotiating point, but **it should not be agreed in isolation from the exclusions, disclosure rules and available security**.

The AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 deductible basket further reduce recovery:
- Smaller losses may be excluded entirely.
- Even qualifying claims produce recovery only above AUD 250,000.
- Related claims could be fragmented to fall below the de minimis.

**Push back:** seek a higher general cap and lower thresholds, with a tipping basket rather than an excess-only basket. Aggregate claims arising from related facts and prevent artificial fragmentation. Thresholds should not apply to fundamental warranties, tax covenant claims, specific indemnities or purchase-price adjustments.

### Fundamental warranties
Capacity and title should not share the general cap or 18-month notification period. A defect in the Seller’s ownership or authority could undermine the acquisition itself.

**Push back:** separate fundamental warranties covering capacity, authority, ownership of all shares, absence of encumbrances and ability to transfer them. Seek recovery up to the full purchase price, without general thresholds, and a substantially longer claim period appropriate to the final execution arrangements and applicable law.

### Tax
Do not accept the assertion that tax is “settled” under the general regime. Pre-Completion tax liabilities may emerge well after 18 months and need not involve a warranty breach.

**Push back:** a separate tax covenant/indemnity for pre-Completion tax and relevant transaction taxes, supported by tax warranties, tailored exclusions and conduct provisions. The claim period should accommodate applicable assessment and reassessment periods, with an appropriate notification buffer.

### Time limits and claim preservation
Eighteen months may leave too little time to identify latent issues. The proposal to apply limitations to every “Claim” could also capture payment obligations, indemnities and completion breaches.

**Push back:**
- Negotiate a longer general warranty period, informed by the accounting and audit cycle.
- Give fundamental, tax and specific indemnity claims their own regimes.
- Permit reasonable notice of contingent claims before loss is quantified.
- Ensure timely notified claims survive expiry; avoid an unduly short deadline to commence proceedings.

### Exclusive remedy and non-reliance
The interaction of clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 could neutralise protections elsewhere in the SPA.

**Push back:** expressly preserve claims for fraud, fraudulent concealment and deliberate misconduct; payment and price-adjustment obligations; specific indemnities; and appropriate equitable relief. Preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Do not assume NSW law will invalidate the Seller’s drafting: resolve the contractual position expressly, including the treatment of misleading or deceptive conduct claims.

## 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: prevent wholesale transfer of diligence risk

Disclosure of the entire data room, documents merely “referred to”, public registers and everything advisers could discover is excessively broad. It could exclude claims without the relevant risk ever having been clearly identified.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter**, preferably against identified warranties.
- Reject blanket disclosure of public records and documents merely referenced elsewhere.
- Identify, freeze and retain the exact disclosed data-room set.
- Reject constructive knowledge and blanket attribution of advisers’ knowledge. Prefer no knowledge exclusion; if conceded, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel and clearly defined facts.
- Prevent disclosure and knowledge provisions from qualifying specific indemnities, fundamental protection or completion obligations unless expressly negotiated.

**Crucially, a disclosure is not a solution.** Known issues may no longer support warranty claims, so they need express completion conditions, price treatment or indemnities. Nor should silence in the Disclosure Letter be treated as evidence that a risk does not exist.

## 3. Bluefen: require effective consent and satisfaction of its conditions

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. There is no final written consent or evidence that its associated conditions have been satisfied.

Reasonable endeavours are not equivalent to an obligation to deliver the required result. Treating the condition as satisfied merely upon delivery of written consent could force Completion with conditional, ineffective or commercially damaging consent.

**Push back:** a Buyer-waivable condition precedent requiring:
- Valid consent from the correct counterparty covering this transaction.
- Satisfaction of all conditions necessary for that consent to be effective.
- No unacceptable amendments, charges, termination rights or other adverse terms.

Require supporting evidence and a long-stop date with appropriate termination rights. Do not accept an indemnity as a routine substitute for protecting this revenue stream.

## 4. Riverlark: repayment and security release at Completion, not afterwards

The approximately **AUD 3.2 million facility remains outstanding**. A promise of post-Completion release leaves the Buyer owning a company exposed to secured debt and possible change-of-control consequences.

**Push back:** obtain a verified payout figure, including interest and fees, and binding lender arrangements for repayment and effective release of all relevant security, guarantees and claims at Completion. Pay the lender directly through the completion funds flow where appropriate.

The debt must reduce the equity consideration under the agreed debt-free/cash-free mechanics. Check carefully that it is **neither omitted nor deducted twice**. Administrative registration of a release can follow where necessary, but the Buyer should not complete with only an unsecured promise to procure discharge.

## 5. Completion bonuses: capture the full cost

The AUD 420,000 bonuses are conditional on Completion and continued employment. That does not establish that they are payable now, but it also does not justify leaving them outside the economics: after Completion, the acquired company may bear the cost.

**Push back:**
- Verify each entitlement, payment date, employment condition and payer.
- Quantify applicable superannuation, payroll tax, withholding and other on-costs.
- Allocate the agreed Seller-borne amounts through transaction-expense/debt-like treatment, a price deduction, direct payment or an appropriately secured reimbursement mechanism.
- Include employment and payroll compliance protection.

Avoid double counting amounts already reflected in working capital or another price adjustment.

## 6. Ironquay: paying SOW3 may not cure the whole IP problem

The disclosed transfer condition depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The AUD 180,000 open balance is evidence requiring investigation—not conclusive proof of non-payment. Equally, there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment.

An indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment may reimburse a fee while leaving the Buyer without usable ownership rights.

**Push back:** verify the payment position and require cleared payment and effective transfer of relevant rights before Completion, supported by a confirmatory assignment where needed. Review the wider chain of title, including relevant subcontractors, background IP and third-party licences.

Seek a specific indemnity covering the disclosed ownership/payment defect and resulting claims, reasonable defence and remediation costs—not merely the outstanding invoice. General IP warranties should remain; protection for a known defect must survive disclosure and knowledge exclusions.

## 7. Export/privacy incident: investigate before accepting the risk

The record establishes an unintended recipient and a potentially affected export of approximately 1,240 records. It does **not** establish access, a notifiable breach or quantified loss. The Seller’s conclusion that it is unlikely to be material is therefore premature.

**Push back:**
- Obtain the investigation findings, access/download logs, containment evidence, actual data scope and recipient response.
- Require a documented assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations, including whether relevant privacy legislation applies.
- Require necessary containment and remediation, preservation of evidence, and Buyer consultation on material communications without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for liabilities and reasonable investigation, notification and remediation costs attributable to the pre-Completion incident, with express treatment of disclosure and knowledge.

If unresolved findings could materially affect the business, negotiate a tailored completion condition or termination right. Do not characterise the event as a confirmed breach without evidence.

## 8. Supplier renewals: investigate substance, not the Seller’s label

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. “Ordinary-course operating costs” is a conclusion, not an established fact.

**Push back:** review DD-008 and DD-011 together for timing, scope, cancellation rights, necessity, approval and accrual. Determine whether these are ordinary future trading costs, pre-Completion liabilities, exceptional commitments or an unapproved acceleration of expenditure.

Apply the appropriate covenant remedy or price treatment only once the facts are established. Ordinary future operating costs should not automatically become Seller debt, but exceptional or improperly incurred commitments should not automatically pass to the Buyer.

## 9. Title and other contractual requirements

### Share title
The share register is relevant evidence, but not a substitute for verification or contractual protection.

**Push back:** reconcile the register with corporate records, issue and transfer history, certificates and relevant security searches. Check options, convertibles, pre-emption rights and other third-party interests. Require transfer of 100% of issued shares free of encumbrances and complete transfer deliverables.

### Office lease and Mossvale
Do not overstate these issues:
- The lease disclosure identifies **notification**, not landlord consent.
- Mossvale’s assignment restriction does not, on the supplied wording, establish a consent requirement for a share sale.

Review the complete agreements for separate change-of-control provisions. Require the notices or consents actually needed, without inventing conditions unsupported by the contracts.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

| Priority | Buyer requirement |
|---|---|
| **Completion protection** | Effective Bluefen consent and satisfaction of its conditions; Riverlark repayment and effective releases; clear share title and material IP ownership protection. |
| **Price integrity** | Reconcile debt, bonuses and on-costs, Ironquay amounts and supplier commitments in a single funds-flow/price-adjustment schedule, without omissions or double counting. |
| **Known-risk allocation** | Specific protection for Ironquay and the export incident; do not rely on warranties already qualified by disclosure. |
| **Meaningful recourse** | Separate fundamental, tax and specific indemnity regimes; reject blanket all-claims limitations and constructive knowledge; tighten disclosure. |
| **Recoverability** | Assess Harbourglass’s ability to meet claims and negotiate escrow, retention or other security where warranted. |

**Bottom line:** resolve business-critical matters before Completion wherever possible, price the liabilities the Buyer is actually assuming, and ensure the remaining remedies cannot be defeated by the Seller’s disclosure and limitation machinery.
